title: Learn SQL from Scratch
subtitle: Ask questions, get answers, from a real database in your browser
description: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, counting, and JOINs, run against a small library database built right into the page. Every answer is checked against real results.

lessons.title: Your First SELECT
lessons.body:
SQL is the language for asking a database questions. A database stores data in **tables**: a table is a grid with named columns and rows, one row per thing. This course runs on two small tables you can inspect under each exercise: `books` and `authors`.

Almost every question starts with the same three words: what, from where, and (sometimes) under what conditions. In SQL that is:

```sql
SELECT * FROM books;
```

Read it aloud: select every column (`*`) from the books table. To take only some columns, name them instead:

```sql
SELECT title, year FROM books;
```

The result is always a fresh grid: the columns you asked for, and the rows that survived your conditions.

exercises.prompt: In SQL, a table is made of…
exercises.explain: A table is a grid: a row per item, a column per property.

exercises.prompt: Show every column of every book.
exercises.explain: SELECT * returns every column of every row.

exercises.prompt: Show only the title and year of each book (in that order).
exercises.explain: Name the columns you want, in the order you want them.

lessons.title: Filtering with WHERE
lessons.body:
Raw SELECT gives you everything. Real questions have conditions, and `WHERE` is where they go:

```sql
SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = 'Fantasy';
```

Text values get single quotes; numbers do not. Beyond `=`, comparisons work the way you expect: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, and `!=` for not equal. Combine conditions with `AND` and `OR`, and flip one with `NOT`:

```sql
SELECT title FROM books WHERE year > 1960 AND pages < 200;
```

One classic beginner slip: forgetting the quotes. `WHERE genre = Fantasy` reads Fantasy as a column name, and the database will complain that no such column exists.

exercises.prompt: List the title of every Fantasy book.
exercises.solution: SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = 'Fantasy'
exercises.explain: The filter kept exactly the two Fantasy rows.

exercises.prompt: List the title and pages of books with more than 300 pages.
exercises.starter: SELECT title, pages FROM books WHERE
exercises.solution: SELECT title, pages FROM books WHERE pages > 300

exercises.prompt: Which keyword introduces a filter condition in a SQL query?
exercises.hint: It comes right after the table name.
exercises.explain: WHERE introduces the condition rows must satisfy.

exercises.prompt: Why does `WHERE genre = Fantasy` fail while `WHERE genre = 'Fantasy'` works?
options: Without quotes, Fantasy is read as a column name, and there is no such column
Fantasy is a reserved word in SQL
Both actually work in every database
exercises.explain: Bare words are identifiers; quoted words are text values.

lessons.title: Sorting and Limiting
lessons.body:
Databases do not promise any natural order. If you want an order, you have to ask for it:

```sql
SELECT title, year FROM books ORDER BY year DESC;
```

`ASC` is ascending (the default when you say nothing), `DESC` is descending. Sorting happens before trimming, so the classic pattern for "top 3 of anything" is sort, then cut:

```sql
SELECT title, pages FROM books ORDER BY pages DESC LIMIT 3;
```

`LIMIT` simply keeps the first N rows of whatever came out. Together, ORDER BY plus LIMIT answers everyday questions like "the five newest", "the three biggest", "the first ten".

exercises.prompt: List the title and year of the five oldest books, oldest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT title, year FROM books ORDER BY year ASC LIMIT 5
exercises.explain: ORDER BY year ASC, then LIMIT 5 keeps the five oldest.

exercises.prompt: List the title and pages of the three longest books, longest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT title, pages FROM books ORDER BY pages DESC LIMIT 3
exercises.explain: Sort by pages DESC, cut to three.

exercises.prompt: If you write ORDER BY without ASC or DESC, which direction do you get?
exercises.explain: ASC is the default sort direction.

lessons.title: Counting and Averaging
lessons.body:
Sometimes the answer is not a list of rows but a single number. Aggregate functions collapse a whole table into one value:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books;
SELECT AVG(pages) FROM books;
```

`COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(column)` counts the rows where that column is not empty, which matters once you meet missing data (NULLs). `SUM` adds a column up, `MIN` and `MAX` find the ends, and `AVG` is the mean. They also combine with WHERE, because the aggregate sees only the filtered rows.

The result of an aggregate query is one row: the function columns you asked for, and nothing else.

exercises.prompt: How many books are in the table? Show just the count.
exercises.hint: COUNT with a star inside parentheses.

exercises.prompt: What is the average page count of all the books? Show just the average.

options: The number of rows in the result
The largest value in the table

lessons.title: Joining Tables
lessons.body:
Real databases split data across tables so nothing is stored twice. Here, each book stores an `author_id` number instead of the author's name, and the names live once in the `authors` table. That number is the thread connecting them.

A `JOIN` follows the thread. You name both tables, and give the rule for matching their rows with `ON`:

```sql
SELECT books.title, authors.name
FROM books
JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id;
```

Read it as: for each book row, find the author row whose `id` equals the book's `author_id`, and stitch them into one output row. Combined with WHERE, you can filter on either side, like "books by Japanese authors", which you will write in the exercise below.

The `books.author_id` = `authors.id` pattern is called a foreign key relationship, and it is the backbone of every serious database you will ever meet.

exercises.prompt: In this database, what connects a book to its author?
options: The book's author_id matches the author's id
The book's title matches the author's name
exercises.explain: A foreign key in one table pointing at a primary key in the other.

exercises.prompt: List every book title together with its author's name.
exercises.solution: SELECT books.title, authors.name FROM books JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id
exercises.explain: Eight books, each stitched to its author.

exercises.prompt: List the titles of books by Japanese authors, along with the author's name. (Filter on authors.country.)
exercises.starter: SELECT books.title, authors.name FROM books JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id
exercises.solution: SELECT books.title, authors.name FROM books JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id WHERE authors.country = 'Japan'
exercises.hint: WHERE works on the joined result, so authors.country is fair game.
exercises.explain: The join stitched the tables, the WHERE kept just Japan.
